course.title: Technical Writing
course.description: How to write documentation that people can use: knowing the reader, choosing the kind of page, writing clear sentences, procedures and reference entries, documenting an API, and testing the result.
course.audience: A capable adult who writes emails and reports well enough and now has to explain a product, process or system to people who did not build it. Engineers, analysts, support staff and career-changers. No documentation tools are assumed; a few lessons read short HTTP, JSON or Markdown snippets.

paragraphs: A page of documentation can be accurate in every sentence and still leave its reader stuck. A setup guide lists three steps where a newcomer needs eight, or a reference entry leaves out a default because it seemed too obvious to mention, and the reader who came to the page with a task in mind has to guess. Technical writing is the craft of writing for that reader, someone who has to act on the page and who arrives without the knowledge the writer takes for granted.

It is hard for the writer, who knows the product better than anyone, and that knowledge is the difficulty: a writer can no longer feel which steps are obvious only to them, so the remedy has to be something we can check rather than feel. We can write down who the reader is and what they already know, and hold each sentence against that, and we can watch a real reader try the task and see where they stop. Many of the checks come down to simple counting, such as the words an edit removed or the share of readers who finished a task, which lets you say whether a page has actually got better.
outcomes: You'll be able to say who a page is for, what they are trying to do, and what they already know.
You'll be able to choose between a tutorial, a how-to guide, a reference page and an explanation, and say why mixing them fails.
You'll be able to turn a passive, vague sentence into a clear one, and measure the change.
You'll be able to write a procedure with one action per step, and a reference entry with every field a reader needs.
You'll be able to document an HTTP API endpoint with its request, response and errors, and test the page with a reader.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on English: Reading, Writing and Rhetoric, How Computers Solve Problems.
introduction.length: 12 lessons, about 12 to 15 minutes each. Each ends with an optional writing task of 5 to 15 minutes.

concepts.title: Audience
concepts.summary: The people who will read a page, defined by what they want to do and what they already know.

concepts.title: Curse of knowledge
concepts.summary: Once you know something it is hard to imagine not knowing it, so you skip steps a newcomer needs.

concepts.title: Reader goal
concepts.summary: The task the reader is trying to finish, which the page exists to serve.

concepts.title: Tutorial
concepts.summary: A guided lesson that takes a beginner through a project to build skill and confidence.

concepts.title: How-to guide
concepts.summary: Steps for a reader who already knows the basics to reach a specific goal.

concepts.title: Reference
concepts.summary: Accurate, complete, neutral description of a thing's parts, looked up rather than read through.

concepts.title: Explanation
concepts.summary: Discussion of why something is as it is, to deepen understanding.

concepts.title: Front-loading
concepts.summary: Put the main point or action at the start of the page, section or sentence.

concepts.title: Heading outline
concepts.summary: Headings that form a hierarchy a reader can scan and a tool can turn into a contents list.

concepts.title: Lists and tables
concepts.summary: Numbered lists for sequences, bulleted lists for sets, tables for items that share several attributes.

concepts.title: Active voice
concepts.summary: A sentence in which the actor is the subject, so the reader knows who or what does the action.

concepts.title: Consistent terminology
concepts.summary: One name for one thing throughout, because a new word suggests a new thing.

concepts.title: Ambiguous pronoun
concepts.summary: A pronoun such as it or this that could point to more than one earlier item.

concepts.title: One idea per sentence
concepts.summary: A sentence that carries a single idea is easier to read and to test.

concepts.title: Parallel structure
concepts.summary: List items that begin with the same grammatical form read as a set.

concepts.title: Flesch reading ease
concepts.summary: 206.835 − 1.015 × (words per sentence) − 84.6 × (syllables per word); higher is easier.

concepts.title: Editing passes
concepts.summary: Separate passes for content, structure, sentence clarity and then correctness of words and punctuation.

concepts.title: Filler
concepts.summary: Words that carry nothing, such as 'in order to', 'it should be noted that' and 'very'.

concepts.title: Reading aloud
concepts.summary: Voicing a draft exposes tangled sentences and missing steps.

concepts.title: One action per step
concepts.summary: Each numbered step asks for one action, so the reader can do it, check it and place themselves in the list.

concepts.title: Prerequisites
concepts.summary: What the reader needs before step 1: access, tools, versions.

concepts.title: Expected result
concepts.summary: What the reader should see after a step or at the end, so they know it worked.

concepts.title: Minimal sample
concepts.summary: A sample with only what the point needs, small enough to read in one glance.

concepts.title: Runnable sample
concepts.summary: A sample that works when copied, including imports and setup, tested at each release.

concepts.title: Show the output
concepts.summary: Giving the result next to the code lets the reader check their run against it.

concepts.title: Reference template
concepts.summary: Every entry has the same fields in the same order so readers can find a detail without reading.

concepts.title: Parameter description
concepts.summary: Each parameter gets a name, type, whether it is required, default and one-sentence description.

concepts.title: Neutral description
concepts.summary: Reference states what is, without instruction or opinion.

concepts.title: Endpoint
concepts.summary: An HTTP method and path that performs one operation, such as GET /v1/items/{id}.

concepts.title: Status code
concepts.summary: The three-digit number in a response: 2xx success, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.

concepts.title: OpenAPI description
concepts.summary: A machine-readable file describing endpoints, parameters and schemas from which reference pages can be generated.

concepts.title: Docs as code
concepts.summary: Writing documentation in plain text files, reviewed and published with the same tools as code.

concepts.title: Style guide
concepts.summary: Agreed rules for terms, tone and formatting, ideally checked by a linter.

concepts.title: Changelog
concepts.summary: A dated list of changes per release, grouped as added, changed, deprecated, removed, fixed and security.

concepts.title: Documentation usability test
concepts.summary: A reader attempts a real task using only the page while an observer watches without helping.

concepts.title: Task success rate
concepts.summary: Participants who finish the task divided by participants who attempted it.

concepts.title: Feedback loop
concepts.summary: Page ratings, search terms and support tickets that show where docs fail after release.

lessons.title: Who is reading, and why

lead.text: The writer's problem has been measured. In 1990 Elizabeth Newton, in her doctoral work at Stanford, asked people to tap out the rhythm of a well-known song on a table while a second person tried to name it from the taps alone. Before the listeners guessed, the tappers were asked how often they expected to be understood, and they said about half the time. In the usual retelling, listeners named 3 songs out of 120.

While tapping, each of them could hear the tune in their head, and that made the taps seem to carry it. The listeners heard only knocks. We call this gap the **curse of knowledge**: once you know something, it is very hard to imagine what it is like not to know it.

afterFigure.text: Notice what the curse does to a writer. It doesn't make you write badly sentence by sentence. It makes you leave out the steps and the words that feel too obvious to mention, and those are exactly the ones a newcomer needs.

lead.text: Start with the **audience**, the people who will read the page. Then ask what each of them is trying to do, which is the **reader goal**, and what they already know when they arrive, which is their **starting knowledge**. Put the three together in one sentence.

Because the reader has used a REST API, the page needn't explain what a request is. Because they have no key yet, the page must start with creating one.

steps.headline: Write an audience statement for a page that begins: "Open the console, find the customer, press Reset."

workedSteps.text: The page tells you who it expects to see it. The words "the customer" and "press Reset" point to someone handling customer accounts.
Next find what the page exists to do. Every step leads to one result, a changed password.
Finally find what the page assumes. It never says where the console is or how to open it, so it assumes the reader has used it.
workedSteps.math: starting knowledge: has used the console

workedSteps.text: Join the three parts in one sentence, and check it by asking whether the page could change if one part changed.
workedSteps.math: "A support agent who has used the console before and needs to reset a customer's password."

reveal.text: A newcomer has to open a terminal, install Node.js, which is the program that provides npm, and get the project onto the machine before the two named actions mean anything. The next screen lists all five.

lead.text: The surest way to catch the curse of knowledge is to do the task the way a newcomer would, writing down every action. Take the line "Navigate to the project folder and run npm start." To the writer it is two actions. To a newcomer it is five: open a terminal, install Node.js, get the project onto the machine, change into its folder, and only then run the command.

afterFigure.text: Notice that nothing in the sentence is wrong. It is correct, and for the writer it is complete. The problem only appears when you ask who is following it, and that is why the audience statement comes first: it tells you which of these five actions you may leave out. For a reader whose statement says they use a terminal daily, the first one can go.

lead.text: What if the page has to serve both a newcomer and an expert? It is tempting to write for everyone, and the result is a page that suits nobody: the newcomer drowns in details and the expert wades through basics. A better habit is to choose a **primary reader**, write the page for that person, and signpost the rest with links such as "New to keys? Read what a key is first" or "Looking for every option? See the reference."

afterFigure.text: This doesn't mean experts want less. They want less about the basics, but they still need exact details such as the name of an option and its default.

blocks.text: Here is a setup page in full: clone the repository, install the dependencies, and start the server. Follow them as a newcomer would, though, and they become eight. You have to find the repository's address, choose a folder for it, install a build tool that "install the dependencies" quietly needs, work out which file starts the server and open it to check that it runs, and those five unwritten actions are exactly the ones a newcomer can't do alone.

Why would a careful writer leave out five of the eight? Someone who knows a task well can no longer feel the gap between what they know and what the page says, so the steps that seem too obvious to mention are the ones that go missing.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to write a one-sentence audience statement for a page and spot the steps a writer has skipped without noticing.
intro.whyItMatters: Every later choice, from the words to the kind of page, is checked against who is reading.

recap.keyIdea: A page serves one reader with one goal and a known starting point, and the curse of knowledge hides the steps that reader is missing.

blocks.text: You saw that people who know something badly overestimate what a newcomer can follow, and that the fix is to write the reader down: who they are, what they want and what they already know. The same habit exposes skipped steps, because you can list what a newcomer would actually do and compare it with what the page says.
When several kinds of reader share a page, choose one and link to the others. An expert still needs exact details, so the statement changes what the page explains, not how careful it is.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson sorts pages into four kinds, because the reader's goal decides which kind they need.

lessons.title: Four kinds of page

lead.text: The four readers in the opening are the ones Daniele Procida described in his Diátaxis framework, which sorts documentation by what the reader needs. A **tutorial** teaches a beginner by guiding them through a small project, so that they build skill and confidence. A **how-to guide** gives steps to a reader who already has the basics and wants a particular result. A **reference** describes the parts of a thing accurately and completely, to be looked up rather than read through. An **explanation** discusses why something is as it is, to deepen the reader's understanding.

afterFigure.text: The map arranges the four along two lines. Across the page, the reader is either studying, which means acquiring a skill, or working, which means applying one. Up and down, they are either doing something or knowing something. Each kind sits where one of each meets, and that is why a page can't serve two without compromising both.

diagram.alt: A two-by-two map. Doing and studying is a tutorial, doing and working is a how-to guide, knowing and studying is an explanation, knowing and working is a reference.

The first sentence settles it. A page that assumes a working pipeline serves a goal for a reader who already has skill.

lead.text: The difference between a tutorial and a how-to guide is easy to miss. A tutorial is a lesson. It chooses one path, shows the reader every step, and says nothing about alternatives, because a beginner who meets three options in step two will stop. A how-to guide is a tool. It assumes the reader knows the basics, names the goal in its title, and gets on with it.

afterFigure.text: Reference leaves out instruction, since a reader checking a default value doesn't want to be taught how to call the function. Explanation leaves out steps, since a reader asking why wants room to think.

steps.headline: Sort the paragraphs of a mixed "Reset a user's password" page.

workedSteps.text: Read each paragraph and ask what the reader of that paragraph wants. Paragraphs 1 to 5 say "click Users", "choose the account", and so on, so they give steps toward one goal.
Paragraphs 6 to 8 say why passwords expire after 90 days, and what attackers do with old ones, so they answer "why".
Paragraphs 9 to 11 list the fields in the password form with their limits, so they exist to be looked up.

lead.text: The reader mid-task has to scroll past a paragraph on why passwords expire to reach step four. The reader checking a field limit has to find it among the steps. The reader who wants the reasons has them cut into pieces by instructions. Splitting the page doesn't remove any material, so nothing is lost; each reader just reaches theirs without crossing the others'.

afterFigure.text: The how-to keeps its five steps and links to the other two pages at the points where a reader might want them. It says to the reader that the reasons exist and where they are, without putting them in the way.

blocks.text: Here are four lines from the documentation of one database product: "Let's build a small chart from a sample file, one step at a time"; "To rotate a key, open Settings, select Keys and click Rotate"; "`max_connections` (integer, default 100): the largest number of open connections"; and "Connections are pooled because opening one costs more than most of the queries it serves." Each is written for a different reader: a beginner who wants to be taught, someone in the middle of a task who wants the next step, someone checking one fact, and someone who wants to know why the product is built the way it is.
Could one page serve all four readers? It would have to teach, direct, list facts and discuss ideas at once, and each of those jobs asks for different writing.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to name which of four kinds a page is and split a page that tries to be several at once.
intro.whyItMatters: Choosing the kind of page first decides what to include and what to leave out.

recap.keyIdea: Documentation comes in four kinds, tutorial, how-to guide, reference and explanation, and a page does its job when it stays one kind.

blocks.text: You sorted pages by what their reader needs: a tutorial builds skill, a how-to guide finishes a task for someone who has the skill, a reference answers a lookup, and an explanation gives reasons. Each leaves out what would slow its reader down, which is why a page that mixes them makes everyone wade through someone else's material.
When you meet a mixed page, decide what it is for, keep that, and move the rest to the page where it belongs with a link between them.

lessons.title: Structure for finding things

lead.text: Look at the two versions in the figure. Both contain the same information, but in the first the setting you want is somewhere in a block of twelve lines of text, and in the second a heading, a short introduction and three numbered steps put it where a scanning eye lands. That difference is what we mean by structure, and none of it needs better sentences. It needs the important things to be placed where a reader will look first.

The habit behind this is called **front-loading**: put the main point or the action at the start of the page, the section and the sentence. In a sentence it means writing "Open Settings to change the timeout" and not "To change the timeout, open Settings", so that a reader who stops after three words has still got the instruction.

reveal.text: The verb gives the reader a task to match against the task in their head. A heading such as "Things to know" gives them nothing to match.

lead.text: A page's headings, read in order, should work as a contents list. That works only when each heading names what is under it and sits at the right level. On a procedure page the headings are tasks, so they begin with verbs: "Create an API key", "Rotate an API key". On a reference page they are the things being described, so they are nouns: "Key length", "Expiry period". Clever headings fail because a scanning reader has no time to decode them.

afterFigure.text: If you could swap a heading for "Things to know" without losing anything, it wasn't naming the content.

reveal.text: The list type is a small promise to the reader. Numbers promise a sequence, and here there is none to promise.

steps.headline: Choose a structure for three plans that each have a name, a cost and a limit.

workedSteps.text: List what is being described. There are three plans, and each has the same three attributes, so the reader will want to compare them.
Ask whether the order matters. The plans may be compared in any order, so numbers would promise a sequence that isn't there.
Ask whether a reader will compare across the items. They will, so the structure has to line each attribute up where it can be compared.
Check against the alternative. Bullets would repeat the three attributes in a line of words for each plan, which is hard to compare.

lead.text: Three kinds of structure cover most of what documentation needs. A **numbered list** is for steps that must be done in order, since it lets a reader say which one they have reached. A **bulleted list** is for a set whose order doesn't matter. A **table** is for items that share several attributes, because each attribute gets a column to compare down.

afterFigure.text: The temptation is to turn everything into bullets, and it costs something. A connected explanation, such as why a cache must be cleared first because stale entries would be served, depends on its "because" and its "so". Cut into bullet fragments it keeps the nouns and loses the argument. Keep short paragraphs for reasoning, one topic in each, and use lists only where the content really is a sequence or a set.

blocks.text: Eye-tracking studies of people reading web pages, reported by the Nielsen Norman Group in 2006, kept finding the same shape. Readers ran their eyes along the first line or two, dropped to read part of a line further down, and then slid down the left edge of the page, so that the places they looked formed a rough letter F.

What does that mean for a page on setting up a proxy? The reader who arrives there usually wants one fact, such as the name of the setting that holds the proxy's address, and they'll find it only if it sits where those eyes land: in a first sentence, a heading or the start of a list item.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to set out a page so a reader can find an answer by scanning: front-loaded sentences, headings that name the content, and the right list or table.
intro.whyItMatters: Most readers scan first, so a page that can be scanned is a page that gets read.

recap.keyIdea: A page is scannable when it front-loads its points, names its sections with verbs or nouns that say what is under them, and uses numbers, bullets or a table to fit the content.

blocks.text: You saw that readers scan along the top and down the left edge, so the main point belongs at the start of the page, the section and the sentence. Headings then work as an outline, with verbs for tasks and nouns for things to look up, and the choice between numbers, bullets and a table depends on whether the content is a sequence, a set or items with several attributes.
Prose stays where the content is reasoning, because a list cuts the connecting words that make an explanation an explanation.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson goes inside the sentence, to the words that make a page clear or vague.

lessons.title: Clear words

lead.text: In "The application saves the file", the thing that acts comes first, then its action, then the thing acted on. We call that **active voice**. In "The file is saved by the application" the order is turned round, and we call it **passive voice**. It is longer, and the actor has been pushed to the end where it can be, and often is, dropped, which is how "The configuration file should be edited" arose.

afterFigure.text: A rule of thumb is to ask "by whom?" at the end of a sentence. If the question has an answer that isn't in the sentence, the actor has gone missing, and you should decide whether to put it back.

diagram.alt: Two orders for one idea. In active voice the actor, the verb and the object appear in that order. In passive voice the object comes first and the actor is last.
diagram.caption: Active puts the actor first. Passive puts the object first and the actor last.

lead.text: Does this mean every passive sentence is a mistake? It doesn't. "The file is deleted after 30 days" is a good sentence, because the reader needs the rule and not the process that carries it out. Passive earns its place when the actor is unknown or unimportant, or when the object is what the sentence is about. Reach for active when the reader has to act, or has to know who is responsible, which in documentation is most of the time.

The verbs deserve the same attention. "Perform an installation of the package" says what "install the package" says, in more words, because the verb has been turned into a noun and a weak verb added to carry it.
In an essay we are taught to vary our words, so that the same noun doesn't come round again and again.

reveal.text: The next screen shows why. A careful reader takes each new word as a sign of a new thing.

lead.text: Literary prose varies its words to avoid repetition. Documentation can't, because the reader has no way to know that "folder", "directory" and "location" are one place. The remedy is **consistent terminology**: pick a name for each thing, use it every time, and, if the product's interface uses a particular word, use that one.

afterFigure.text: The same goes for names of things in the product. If the button says Build, the page says Build, not "the compile button" in one place and "the run action" in another.

lead.text: Pronouns cause trouble because the writer knows what "it" refers to and the reader has to work it out. In "The script reads the config and writes the log. It fails if missing," the word "it" could mean the script, the config or the log, and "missing" fits only one of them. We call a pronoun like this an **ambiguous pronoun**. The same happens with "this" at the start of a sentence, as in "Click the button. This starts the build."

afterFigure.text: The cure is almost always to use the noun again. "Click Build. The build starts a new container" has no pronoun, and every sentence in it can be understood on its own.

steps.headline: Rewrite "Click the button. This starts the build."

workedSteps.text: Ask what "this" could point to. It could be the click, the button, or the whole action.
Decide what you meant. The writer meant the click makes the build start, so the subject is the build.
Replace that word with the noun it was meant to stand for, and name the button so the instruction can be followed.
workedSteps.math: "Click Build. The build starts a new container."

workedSteps.text: Check each sentence on its own. Neither needs the other to be understood.

reveal.text: Three of the four verbs name no actor, so the paragraph leaves the reader to guess who restarted the server, who cleared the cache and who rotated the logs.
Each wrong choice drops the server, turns the verb into a noun, or keeps the passive. Only the answer puts the server first as the one doing the validating.
Passive is a tool, not a fault. What the reader needs decides whether the actor belongs in the sentence.

lessons.orientation: Turn passive, vague or inconsistent sentences into clear ones with active verbs, one term per thing and no ambiguous pronouns.
lessons.nextAction: Shorten sentences, give each paragraph one topic and measure readability with the Flesch score.

blocks.text: Here is a sentence that could be in almost any set of instructions: "The configuration file should be edited." It reads easily enough, so what is wrong with it? Try to answer a question about it. Who edits the file? The sentence knows, but it doesn't say, and a reader who has to guess will sometimes guess wrong.

Leaving out the actor is one of a few small habits that account for much of the difference between a page that is clear and one that merely looks correct. Using different words for the same thing is another, and so is writing "it" or "this" where the word could point to any of several earlier nouns.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to rewrite a passive sentence so its actor is clear, use one word for one thing, and replace a vague pronoun with the noun it stands for.
intro.whyItMatters: Clear words cost the writer a little attention and save every reader from guessing.

recap.keyIdea: Name the actor, use one word for one thing, and replace ambiguous pronouns with nouns, keeping passive for sentences where the actor does not matter.

blocks.text: You looked at three habits that make a page look correct and read badly: leaving out the actor, varying a word for style, and using a pronoun that could point to several nouns. Each hides something the reader needs, and each is fixed by saying the thing again, plainly.
Passive voice survives where the actor is unknown or unimportant, because the aim isn't a rule against it but a page that tells the reader who does what whenever that matters.

lead.text: Compare the long sentence in the opening with the same material cut into four, as in the figure: "Does your version predate 2.0, and have you set a proxy in the settings file? That file lives in your home directory. Before you upgrade, back up the file and note down the proxy address. The installer replaces the file and keeps none of the old values." Nothing of substance has been dropped, and each sentence now holds one thing. We call that **one idea per sentence**, and it's easy to test: if you can't say what a sentence is about in a few words, it is probably about several things.

afterFigure.text: Notice also that the instruction now sits at the start of its sentence, after only a short condition. Splitting is rarely about making things shorter for their own sake. It is about putting each piece where the reader is ready for it.

lead.text: The same idea, that the reader should be able to predict the next piece, applies to lists. In the first list in the figure each item begins with a verb that names an action: install, configure, run. This is **parallel structure**. In the second list, the middle item turns into an -ing form and the last into a passive sentence, so the reader keeps checking whether each item is a step, a heading or a description.

afterFigure.text: Parallel structure also makes errors visible. If three items start with verbs and the fourth starts with a noun, the odd one stands out.

reveal.text: The test is mechanical: read only the first word of each item.
Shorter sentences lower one of the two penalties, so the score goes up. The next screen gives the formula, and the two penalties turn out to be very different in size.

lead.text: Rudolf Flesch published his Reading Ease formula in 1948, and it is still the standard quick measure. It takes the average number of words per sentence, W, and the average number of syllables per word, S, and computes 206.835 − 1.015 × W − 84.6 × S. The result is a **Flesch reading ease** score. Scores in the 60s are usually called plain English, and scores below 30 are very hard.

afterFigure.text: Look at the two cases in the figure. Both have 20 words per sentence, so the sentence term is the same, 20.3. When the words get a tenth of a syllable shorter, the syllable term drops from 126.9 to 118.44, a difference of 8.46, and the score rises from 59.635 to 68.095. A tenth of a syllable is worth more than eight points, while a whole extra word per sentence costs only about one.

lead.text: As one sentence of 52 words, with 1.6 syllables per word, the opening example scores 206.835 − 52.78 − 135.36, which is about 19.

reveal.text: Splitting made no words shorter, and it still lifted the score by roughly 39 points, because sentence length is the only thing that changed.

lead.text: Is a high score a sign of good writing? Look at the two lines in the figure. "Press Save to keep your work" and "Press Save to wipe your work" have the same number of words and the same word lengths, so they score the same, although only one of them matches what the button does. The formula counts letters and sentences. It can't check accuracy, or whether a word such as "authentication", which is long and also necessary, will be understood by this reader.

afterFigure.text: The score also rewards the wrong thing if you chase it. A string of very short sentences scores well and loses the connections between ideas, which is the "because" and "so" that make a paragraph an explanation. Use the number as a smoke alarm.

blocks.text: Here is a sentence of the kind that turns up in real documentation: If you use a version released before 2.0 and have set a proxy in the settings file, which lives in your home directory, then before you upgrade you should back up that file and note down the proxy address, because the installer replaces the file and keeps none of the old values. Read it once, and then try to say aloud what you are meant to do.

Most people find they have to go back to the start, even though nothing in the sentence is wrong and every word does some work. Why is it hard, then? The sentence asks the reader to hold several things at once, while a page is easier to use when it hands them over one at a time.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to split an overloaded sentence, make a list parallel, and compute a Flesch reading ease score and say what it does and does not tell you.
intro.whyItMatters: Short sentences and a measurable score give you something to check when a page feels hard.

recap.keyIdea: A sentence is clear when it carries one idea, its lists run in parallel, and a Flesch score can check its length without judging whether it is right.

blocks.text: You split a 52-word sentence into four, put conditions before actions, and made list items begin the same way. Then you computed reading ease from words per sentence and syllables per word, and saw that a tenth of a syllable counts for far more than an extra word.
The score is a useful alarm that cannot tell right from wrong, and very short sentences lose the connections that carry an explanation.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson puts these skills into a routine: editing a draft in separate passes, and measuring how much you cut.

lessons.title: Editing a draft

lead.text: Suppose you fix the commas in a paragraph, and then decide the whole paragraph isn't needed. The commas cost you time and taught you nothing. The remedy is to edit in **passes**, each looking for one kind of fault. First, decide what the reader must do or know, and delete the rest. Second, check the order and the headings. Third, work through sentences and words, using the habits from the last three lessons. Fourth, check the small facts: names, numbers, links and any step that refers to another.

afterFigure.text: The order is the point. The first pass can remove paragraphs, so you don't polish them. The second can move them, so you don't tidy words that are about to move. By the fourth pass nothing large will change, and so checking a number can't be undone by a later edit.

reveal.text: Cutting content first means every later pass has less to work on.
The edit removed 12 words, which is 30% of the paragraph. The next screen shows how to work out that percentage, so that edits of different lengths can be compared.

lead.text: Look at the 15-word instruction in the figure. The shaded words, "In order", "it is necessary that you" and "the following", can go with no loss, because what the reader has to do is carried by "start the server" and "run". We call words of that kind **filler**. They tend to appear in the same few phrases, such as "in order to", "it should be noted that" and "very", which is why they are worth learning to spot.

afterFigure.text: To measure a cut, take the words removed and divide by the length you started with. A 20-word paragraph cut to 12 has lost 8 words, and 8 ÷ 20 is 0.4, so 40% of it was filler.

Subtract to find the words removed.
Check what was removed. "In order", "it is necessary that you" and "the following" can all go, because the reader would not miss any of them.
Divide by the original length and turn the result into a percentage.

steps.headline: Measure a second cut: a 60-word paragraph edited down to 45.

workedSteps.text: Words removed: subtract the new length from the old.
The share removed is those 15 words divided by the original 60, written as a percentage.

lead.text: Shortness is not the goal. The goal is a page that keeps what the reader needs, and a hurried edit can cut a word that was doing real work. "Do not delete the backup" loses its point if "Do not" goes. "Wait 30 seconds" shortened to "wait" has lost a number the reader acts on, and "version 2.0 or later" is no longer true as "a later version".

afterFigure.text: So each cut gets one test: would the reader do something different without this word? If so, the word is a fact and stays. If not, it is filler and can go, which is why "very" and "in order to" are safe, while "not" never is.

reveal.text: A shorter page is only better when it says the same things. That is why the third pass uses the earlier lessons and the fourth checks facts.

lead.text: Two habits finish the work. Read the draft aloud, or have someone else read it to you. A sentence that makes you stumble or take a breath in the wrong place is usually tangled, and a step that you have to skip over to make sense of the next one is a step that is missing. The ear picks up what the eye, which has seen the draft many times, has stopped noticing.

afterFigure.text: Then do the fourth pass, which is about small facts. Check that the product name is spelled and capitalised as it appears on screen, that each number matches the software, and that each link still goes where it says.

reveal.text: Notice that the warning kept the cut from reaching 28%. A careful edit often removes less than the most it could.

lessons.orientation: Edit a draft in four passes, cut filler without losing facts, and measure the cut as a percentage.
lessons.nextAction: Write a numbered procedure with one action per step, the where before the what, and the result stated.

blocks.text: Here is a sentence from a first draft: "In order to start the server, it is necessary that you run the following command." It has 15 words, and it can be written in seven, "To start the server, run this command", without losing anything the reader needs.

The padding was easy to see here because the sentence stood alone. Spread across a whole draft it is much harder to spot, particularly while you are also worrying about commas, headings and whether the steps are in the right order, which is why it pays to go through a draft several times with one concern at a time.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to edit a draft in four passes, cut filler without losing a fact, and say how much you cut as a percentage.
intro.whyItMatters: Separate passes stop small fixes from hiding large faults, and a measured cut shows the edit was real.

recap.keyIdea: Edit in four ordered passes, cut only words that carry no fact, and measure the cut as words removed divided by words you started with.

blocks.text: You edited in passes, deciding content first and checking small facts last, so that each decision came before the work that depended on it. Filler such as "in order to" could go, and the size of a cut was the words removed divided by the original length: 8 of 15 words, about 53%.
The cut had one limit. A warning, a number or a condition is a fact, so it stays whatever the length, and reading the draft aloud helps catch a step that has gone missing.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson applies all of this to one kind of page, the procedure, where each step must be a single action the reader can check.

lessons.title: Writing a procedure

lead.text: The reason is practical. In the figure, the packed step hides which action failed, and the reader has to start again from the top. Split into three steps, a failure at step 3 shows that steps 1 and 2 worked. This is the rule of **one action per step**. It also gives the reader a way back in: someone who looks up from the screen can say "I'm on step 2" and continue from there.

afterFigure.text: Each step also begins with a verb in the imperative, such as "Open", "Select" or "Click", because the reader is being told what to do.

lead.text: Compare "In the File menu, click Save" with "Click Save in the File menu". The first sends them to the File menu, and the action arrives when they're looking at the right place. The rule is **location first**, and it applies to any step that has both.

lead.text: Put the **prerequisites** first, before step 1: the access, the tools and the software versions the reader needs. A reader who learns on step 6 that they need an administrator account has already half-changed their system. Then state the **expected result** for any step where the reader can't tell by looking whether it worked, as in "The status changes to Running within 30 seconds." Without that line, a silent failure and a slow success look the same.

blocks.text: Take a step from a procedure that looks perfectly tidy: "Open Settings, select Network, and click Reset." Now suppose the reader follows it and nothing happens. Did Settings fail to open, was there no Network entry on their version, or did the Reset button do nothing? The step contains three possible failures, and the reader can't tell which one they met.

A procedure is the one kind of page that a reader follows while doing something else, with their eyes going back and forth between the page and the screen. The page has to let the reader do one thing, check it, and find their place again, and it has to tell them what they will see when each thing works.

blocks.text: You took a packed step apart and saw that a failure at the end of one tells the reader nothing, whereas three single-action steps show where they got to. Each step starts with a verb, puts its location or condition first, and, where the reader cannot tell by looking, ends with the result they should see.
Prerequisites go before step 1 so that no one discovers a missing tool halfway through, and troubleshooting goes after the list so that it stays out of the way until it is needed.

lead.text: A page might show 40 lines to teach one idea, and the reader has to work out which 8 matter. A **minimal sample** is trimmed to those 8: the one call being taught, the setup it can't work without, and nothing else. The test for each line is whether the reader would miss it. A line for logging, or for a feature the page isn't about, is a line the reader has to read, wonder about and rule out.

afterFigure.text: Reducing the sample doesn't weaken it. It points at the part that matters, and a reader who wants the rest can follow a link to a fuller example.

lead.text: A sample that stops at the command leaves the reader guessing: did it work, and what should they have seen? Show the result immediately after the code. The reader can then compare line by line, and a difference between what they got and what the page shows is the start of a diagnosis.
Explain the idea once, in a sentence before or after the sample, instead of commenting on every line. A sample where each line carries a comment is harder to read than the code.

steps.headline: Work out the output of a complete sample.

workedSteps.text: The sample is: `import json`, then `data = json.loads('{"a": 1, "b": 2}')`, then `print(data['b'])`. The import makes `json` available.
`json.loads` turns the text into a dictionary, Python's table of keys and the value stored under each, here with the keys `a` and `b`.
`print(data['b'])` looks up the key `b` in that dictionary.

lead.text: A reader who has used one entry has learned the layout of every other, if the layout is fixed. The **reference template** for a function has six fields: its name, its purpose in one sentence, its parameters, what it returns, the errors it can raise, and an example. The order never changes.

afterFigure.text: The template also makes gaps visible. If one entry has no errors field, the reader can't tell whether the function never fails or the writer forgot.

lead.text: Each parameter gets one row: its name, its type, whether it is required, its default and a one-sentence description. In the figure the retries row reads "retries, integer, no, 3, tried again after a failure", so a reader who wants to know what happens when it is omitted reads along one row and has it. A table rather than prose lets them scan down a column too, to see which parameters are required.

afterFigure.text: Reference is neutral: it says what is true and doesn't instruct or advise. "The largest file, in megabytes, that one upload may send" is a description. "You should raise this if your users send video" is advice, and belongs in a how-to. Notice that the description gives the unit, megabytes, because a bare 10 could mean megabytes or kilobytes.

lead.text: Consistency is the template's second job. If the retries parameter is described in seconds on one page and milliseconds on another, readers can't trust either. Use the same field names, the same order and the same wording for the same ideas across entries, and treat a difference as a fault until it is shown to be real.

afterFigure.text: Reference also resists growing. When a parameter needs a paragraph on when to use it, write that in a how-to or an explanation and link to it from the row.

blocks.text: Here is one row from the reference page of an HTTP client library: retries | integer | no | 3, followed by "The number of times a failed request is tried again before an error is raised." Nobody reads a row like that as part of the page from the top down. A reader arrives at it with one question in mind, finds the word `retries`, and reads across.

That is the kind of page the second lesson called reference, one that is looked up and not read through. What makes looking up quick is regularity, since when every entry has the same fields in the same order, a reader who has found one fact in one entry knows where to look for the same fact in every other.

recap.keyIdea: A reference entry has the same six fields in the same order, and each parameter row gives its type, whether it is required, its default and a neutral one-sentence description.

blocks.text: You saw that lookup depends on regularity: the same six fields in the same order, and a parameter row with five columns that put the default beside the name. A description states what is true, with its unit, and doesn't advise; advice goes in a how-to and reasons in an explanation, both reached by a link.
The template also shows what is missing, since an empty field can be counted and a gap in prose can't.

lessons.title: Documenting an HTTP API

lead.text: An **endpoint** is an HTTP method and a path that together perform one operation, such as `GET /v1/items/{id}`. The method says what kind of operation it is, and the path says on what. A reader who comes to the page for one endpoint wants six things: what it does, the method and path, how to authenticate, the parameters, what the response looks like, and an example.

afterFigure.text: Most writers document the Responses row for the success case alone, and then the page is full only where the reader needs it least. The errors are what a reader looks up when something goes wrong, so the row has to list each error status, what causes it and what to do.

reveal.text: Together the method and the path identify the endpoint, which is why both belong in the page's title.
The usual code is 204 No Content, a success that says the body is empty on purpose. The next screen sets out the families of status codes, so you can see where it fits.

lead.text: Every HTTP response begins with a **status code**. The first digit sorts them into families. Codes starting with 2 mean success, those starting with 4 mean the client sent something wrong, and those starting with 5 mean the server failed. An API page needs a short list from them: 200, 201 and 204 for success; 400, 401, 403, 404 and 429 for the client's errors; and 500 for the server's.

afterFigure.text: Choosing the code that matches is part of the documentation. A 200 for a created item is accurate but less exact than 201, and a 400 for an expired key points the reader at their request when the fault is their credentials. Use the buttons to see each family.

reveal.text: The first digit settles the family, and the meaning settles the code.

lead.text: The error rows are the heart of the Responses section. Each gets its status code, a one-line cause and the fix. The commonest confusion is between 401 and 403. A 401 means the request lacks valid credentials: the key is missing, wrong or expired, and the server can't tell who is asking. A 403 means the credentials are valid but don't allow this action, so the server knows who is asking and still refuses.

afterFigure.text: The fixes differ, which is why the page can't treat them alike. For a 401 the reader gets a new or refreshed key. For a 403 a new key would not help, since they need the permission added. Put a single error format on every response, with a code, a message and a hint for the fix, and document it once. A 429 has a fix of its own, which is to wait, and many APIs say how long in a Retry-After header, giving the number of seconds.

steps.headline: Document POST /v1/items, a call that creates an item.

workedSteps.text: Start with the method and path in the title, then one sentence of purpose.
State the authentication: a Bearer key with write permission.

List the success response first: 201 Created with the new item. Then each error with its cause: 400 for a missing name, 403 for a key that cannot write, 429 for too many calls, and one more for a key that has been revoked.
For the revoked key, give the status code that tells the reader to get a new key and send the request again.

lead.text: Many teams keep their endpoint facts in an **OpenAPI description**: a file listing each path, its methods, its parameters and its responses. In the snippet, the lines under `responses` declare the four codes that `POST /v1/items` can return. Tools turn a file like this into reference pages, which keeps the facts consistent with the product.

afterFigure.text: What a generated page can't supply is the guidance. The file says that 401 is "key is expired", and a person has to write what the reader does next, when to use the endpoint and how it fits with others.

diagram.alt: A short OpenAPI snippet for POST /v1/items. It gives a summary and lists four responses: 201 Created, 400 name is missing, 401 key is expired and 403 key cannot write.

blocks.text: Here is an API page that documents one call: send a POST to /v1/items with a name, and you get back the new item. It is accurate and tidy, and it covers only the part a reader usually gets right on the first try. When the reader's key expires and the call returns a 401, the page has nothing to say about what a 401 means or what to do about it, so it answers a question the reader didn't have and none of the one they do.
Every HTTP response begins with a three-digit status code, and when something goes wrong that number, with the error body that follows it, is what the reader comes to the page to look up.

lessons.title: Docs as code and review

lead.text: The pages are plain-text files, usually Markdown, and they sit beside the code in its repository, the store that keeps every past version of the project. A change to either goes through a **pull request**, in which a teammate reads it before it is merged. Because the files are text, the same tools work on them: you can see exactly what changed between versions, go back to an earlier one, and run automatic checks whenever someone proposes an edit. This arrangement is what people call **docs as code**.

afterFigure.text: The gain is that a change to the flag and the change to its page can travel in one pull request, so the reviewer sees both at once and neither can be forgotten. Step through the path in the figure: the docs follow the same road as the code, and every stop on it is a chance to catch a fault.

diagram.alt: A five-step path a docs change takes: write the change, open a pull request, automatic checks, review, merge and publish. One step is highlighted in each view.

lead.text: Teams that write together need agreed rules, such as whether to say "select" or "click on", whether to use "please" in instructions, and how headings nest. These form a **style guide**. A written guide helps, but reviewers can't remember all of it, and checking it by eye is tedious work. So the rules that can be checked by machine are given to a **linter**, a tool that reads the files and reports each break with its file and line number. Prose linters such as Vale do this for documentation.

afterFigure.text: Once the linter has dealt with terms and formatting, the person reading the pull request can spend their attention on what a machine can't judge: whether the page suits its reader and whether the steps work.

lead.text: Treating review as proofreading misses the point. A reviewer who runs the steps finds the missing flag, the renamed option and the command that only works on the author's machine, and a proofreader can't see any of them because the page reads well. A useful checklist has four questions: does the page match its audience statement, is each fact correct for this version, do the steps run as written, and do the links go where they say.

afterFigure.text: Documentation also has to stay matched to the product. If a page describes version 2.0, keep it with the 2.0 code, and when 3.0 ships, branch the docs with it, so that a reader on the older version isn't told about options that don't exist for them.

lead.text: A **changelog** isn't a copy of the commit log. The commit log is written for the developers, with messages such as "wip" and "refactor: rename helper", most of which no user could act on. A changelog gives a dated heading for each release, and below it the changes grouped under Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed, Fixed and Security. Each entry says what changed for the user and, where they must do something, what that is.

afterFigure.text: The grouping is the useful part. A reader upgrading looks first under Removed and Security, because those are the headings that can break their setup or need quick action.

steps.headline: Write the changelog entry for a release that removes the v1 /items endpoint.

workedSteps.text: Decide who reads it. Ask who is affected when the endpoint goes, and what they need to know about their calls.
Choose the heading. The endpoint has gone, so the entry belongs under Removed.
Say what changed in the user's terms, and what they should do about it.
Add it under the release's dated heading, in the ISO date format.

reveal.text: Notice that the right line says what to do next. That is the difference between recording a change and telling users about it.

blocks.text: When a command-line tool renames its flag `--out` to `--output`, the change to the code goes through the usual process: a developer writes it, a colleague reviews it, the tests pass, and it ships. The setup guide that still says `--out` goes through none of that, because it lives in a wiki that nobody reviews and no test knows about.

The cause is where the page lives. Code is written in plain text, kept in version control, changed through reviewed proposals and checked automatically before it ships, and documentation that sits outside all of that falls behind it. The remedy is to give the documentation the same home, which is what people mean by treating docs as code.

intro.whyItMatters: Documentation that travels with the code is reviewed with it, and so stays true to it.

recap.keyIdea: Docs as code keeps pages in version control, checks style with a linter, reviews by running the steps, and records changes for users in a changelog.

blocks.text: You followed a docs change along the path a code change takes: a pull request, automatic checks from a linter that enforces the style guide, and a review that runs the steps, since proofreading can't tell that a command fails. Together they keep a page in step with the product it describes.
The changelog tells users what changed under six headings, and the entries are written for them, which is why it isn't a copy of the commit log.

lessons.title: Testing documentation with readers

lead.text: The test has three parts: a task, a participant and an observer. First choose one page and one task that it should enable. Then recruit someone who matches the audience statement you wrote in the first lesson, because a colleague who built the product will skip the very steps you want to test. Then have them try the task using only the page, while an observer writes down where they stop, hesitate or go back, and says nothing.

afterFigure.text: That silence is the hard part. When the reader frowns, you will want to explain, and once you do, the test is over, because the real reader never gets an explanation. Everything you learn from this **documentation usability test** comes from the moment the reader is stuck.

lead.text: Two numbers come out of a test. The **task success rate** is the number who finished divided by the number who attempted the task, expressed as a percentage. If 7 of 10 finish, the rate is 70%. The second number is a place: the step where the others stopped, which is the **first point of failure**. In the figure, ten readers start, all ten reach step 3, and two stop at step 4.

afterFigure.text: The two readers stopped at step 4 because the page assumed a tool was already installed, which is the curse of knowledge from the first lesson showing up in a measurement. A rate by itself tells you something is wrong. The point of failure tells you what.

lead.text: A test often finds several faults. In the figure, six readers stopped at step 4 and one stopped at step 7. It is tempting to fix whichever is easiest, or whatever you noticed first, but the count gives a better order. Fixing step 4 helps six readers and fixing step 7 helps one, so step 4 comes first, and when it is fixed you test again to see where the next drop falls.

afterFigure.text: The order of the tests also matters. Retesting with new participants is better than asking the same people to try again, since they now know what the page meant.

steps.headline: Analyse a test in which 10 readers attempt a task. Three stop at step 2 and two stop at step 6.

workedSteps.text: Count who finished. Ten attempted, and 3 + 2 = 5 stopped, so 5 finished.
Divide the number who finished by the number who attempted.
Find the first point of failure, which is the earliest step where readers drop.
Decide the order of fixes. Step 2 stopped three readers and step 6 stopped two, so step 2 is fixed first, then the test is run again.

steps.headline: Analyse a second test, with 15 readers attempting a task, of whom 9 finish.

workedSteps.text: Divide the number who finished by the number who attempted.
That division gives a fraction of the readers, and the success rate writes it as a percentage.

lead.text: Once the page is public, other signals take over. Page ratings say which pages disappoint. Search terms show what readers look for and don't find. Support tickets show the questions the docs did not answer, and a cluster of tickets on one error is a hint that the troubleshooting page lacks it. Together these form a **feedback loop**: you publish, readers use the page, the signals come back, and you fix the page.

afterFigure.text: Read the signals with care. A page with few views might be unneeded, but it might just be hard to find, and the search terms and tickets show which.

lessons.orientation: Plan a documentation test with a reader, compute a task success rate and decide what to fix first.
lessons.nextAction: Write a page for a named reader, choose its kind, structure it, edit it, document an endpoint and test it with a real reader.

blocks.text: Ask someone who has just used a page whether it was clear, and most will say yes. They want to be polite, and the page did get them somewhere, or they think it did. What they cannot tell you is what they didn't understand, since a reader doesn't notice a gap that they've filled with a guess.

Watching someone try to finish a task produces something different, because you see what they do and not what they say. When a reader reaches step 4 and stops, you know exactly where the page failed, and you can see whether the cause is a missing prerequisite, a term they didn't know or a step that assumed a skill.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to plan a test with a real reader, compute the task success rate, find the first point of failure and choose which fix comes first.
intro.whyItMatters: A test with a real reader tells you what a page does, which no amount of rereading can.

recap.keyIdea: Watch a real reader attempt a task, compute the success rate and the first point of failure, and fix the failure that stops the most readers first.

blocks.text: You tested a page by watching a reader who matched the audience statement try a task without help, and you counted the result as a success rate, with the step where the others stopped. The count decided the order of fixes, so the failure that stopped six readers came before the one that stopped one.
After release the loop continues through ratings, search terms and support tickets, which you read with care, since a page with few views may be hard to find and not unneeded.

questions.prompt: The tappers expected listeners to name the song 50% of the time, and in the retelling 3 of 120 listeners did. About how many times higher was the expectation than the result?
hints: Start by turning 3 of 120 into a percentage.
Divide 3 by 120 and multiply by 100.
Now divide the expected 50% by that result.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 3 of 120 is 2.5%, and 50 ÷ 2.5 = 20, so the expectation was twenty times too high.

questions.onCorrect: The expectation was 20 times the result. The tappers could not feel the gap, because they heard the whole tune while they tapped.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the result by the expectation. Put the larger figure, 50, on top.
That is the difference between the two percentages. The question asks how many times higher, which needs a division.

questions.prompt: A page says "Navigate to the project folder and run npm start." Someone who has never set up the project follows it on a new laptop. How much will they have to do beyond the two actions the line names?
hints: What does the line assume is already on the machine?
Where does the npm command come from on a new laptop?

acceptedIdeas: Several actions the line never mentions
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Several actions the line never mentions

questions.onCorrect: There are five actions in all, and three of them go unmentioned because the writer's own machine had them done long ago.

misconceptions.feedback: A new laptop may have no Node.js, the program that provides npm, and no copy of the project, so the line depends on actions it never names.
Installing Node.js, which provides npm, is one unwritten action, and opening a terminal and getting the project onto the machine are two more.

choices.label: One small extra action at most
Nothing more, since the line names every action
Several actions the line never mentions

questions.prompt: The statement "A data analyst who wants to export last month's sales report" names a reader and a goal. What is the name of the third part of an audience statement, the one it leaves out?
hints: A statement has three parts: who, what they want, and one more.
The part you most need in order to decide which steps to include.
questions.onCorrect: Without starting knowledge the writer cannot tell which steps are obvious to this reader and which must be written out.

misconceptions.feedback: The reader is already named, as a data analyst. The missing part is about what that person already knows.
The goal is there: export last month's sales report. Look for the part about prior experience.

questions.prompt: The task the reader is trying to finish, and which the page exists to serve, is called the reader's what?
hints: It is what the reader wants to have done when they leave the page.
questions.onCorrect: A page earns its place by getting the reader to their goal, which is why the goal belongs in the audience statement.

questions.prompt: A page says "Deploy by pushing your branch." A newcomer actually has to do five things: add the remote, authenticate, create a branch, push it and watch the build. The page names two of them. How many go unwritten?
hints: Count what the newcomer must do, then what the page says.
The total is five and the page names two.
Subtract the written actions from the total.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 5 − 2 = 3 actions are left for the reader to guess.

questions.onCorrect: Each unwritten action is a place where a newcomer stops, and the writer rarely notices because the writer does them without thinking.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number the page does name. The question asks for the ones it leaves out.

questions.prompt: A page on rotating an API key has this audience statement: "A developer who has used a REST API before, wants to rotate an API key, and has never rotated one." The page is now rewritten for a senior administrator who has rotated keys for years and still needs the exact option names. Which edit to the audience statement fits?

choices.label: Change the starting knowledge to "has rotated keys before"
Change the goal to "learn what a key is"
Change the reader to "everyone who uses keys"
Drop the statement, since experts need no audience

hints: Which of the three parts differs for this reader?
The task is the same, so something else moves.

acceptedIdeas: Change the starting knowledge to "has rotated keys before"
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Change the starting knowledge to "has rotated keys before"

questions.onCorrect: Experts want less about the basics but still need exact details, so only the starting knowledge changes.

misconceptions.feedback: The goal is still to rotate a key. It is the starting knowledge that has changed.
A mixed reader leads to a page that suits nobody. Keep one primary reader.
Experts are an audience too. They need fewer basics but exact details.

questions.prompt: In Newton's tapping study as retold, 3 of 120 listeners named the song. What percentage is that?
hints: Divide 3 by 120.
That gives a decimal; a percentage is that decimal times 100.
0.025 times 100 is the answer.
questions.onCorrect: Tappers had predicted 50%, so what the listener experienced was a fraction of what the tapper imagined.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the fraction. Multiply by 100 for a percentage.
Check the decimal place: 3 ÷ 120 is 0.025.

questions.prompt: In Newton's tapping study, tappers expected listeners to name the song about half the time, and in the usual retelling 3 of 120 did. Why did the tappers expect so much more?
hints: What could the tapper hear that the listener couldn't?
questions.onCorrect: That is the curse of knowledge at work: the tune the tapper could hear was never in the taps at all.

misconceptions.feedback: The songs were well known ones, so the tappers' expectation did not come from the choice of song.
Effort does not change the result, because a rhythm without its tune carries far less of a song than the tappers believed.
A rhythm can be tapped accurately and still fail to identify a song, so the cause lies elsewhere.

acceptedIdeas: Only the tappers could hear the tune while they tapped
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only the tappers could hear the tune while they tapped

choices.label: The songs were less well known than the tappers had assumed
The listeners did not try hard enough to name the songs
Tapping out a rhythm accurately is harder than it looks
Only the tappers could hear the tune while they tapped

questions.prompt: Which is the best audience statement for a page on resetting passwords?

choices.label: A support agent who has used the admin console every day for several years
A support agent new to the admin console who must reset a customer's password
A support agent with a customer waiting who needs to reset a password today
Everyone who uses the product, whether they are new to it or experienced

hints: A good statement names who, what they want and what they know.
Check each option for all three parts.

acceptedIdeas: A support agent new to the admin console who must reset a customer's password
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A support agent new to the admin console who must reset a customer's password

questions.onCorrect: It names a reader, a goal and a starting point, so every later choice about the page can be checked against it.

misconceptions.feedback: This names a reader and what they know, but not what they want to do. Without the goal the writer can't tell which steps the page needs.
This names a reader and a goal, but not what the reader already knows, so the writer can't tell which steps are obvious to them.
A statement for everyone gives the writer nothing to decide with, so the page ends up suiting nobody.

questions.prompt: The difficulty of imagining not knowing what you know is called the curse of what?
hints: The word is the thing the writer has too much of.
questions.onCorrect: Because the curse is invisible from the inside, the fix is to check the page against a real reader.

questions.prompt: A page is titled "Build your first dashboard". It guides a beginner through one small project from start to finish. Which of the four kinds is it?
hints: It teaches a newcomer by having them do something together with the page.
questions.onCorrect: A tutorial is judged by what the learner can do afterwards. The dashboard is only the vehicle.

misconceptions.feedback: A how-to guide assumes its reader already has the basics, and this page takes a beginner through a project so that they learn.
A reference page is looked up for facts, and this page leads a beginner through a project from start to finish.
An explanation discusses why something is as it is, and this page has the reader build something step by step.

Explanation
How-to guide
